note: Books are reading paths, not proofs. Each entry carries the question it is good at asking. Trajectories are past moments that rhyme with a present headline; a rhyme is not a cause. Extended on 27 October 2026 with the trajectories the readings’ horizons draw on; every link checked.

books.title: The Glass Bead Game
books.author: Hermann Hesse
books.question: What is gained, and what is lost, when every field of knowledge is played as one game of connections?
books.why: The site's own founding charter and its own warning. Castalia plays beautifully and forgets the world outside the walls.

books.title: Imagined Communities
books.author: Benedict Anderson
books.question: How do millions of strangers come to feel they share one story, read at the same hour?
books.why: Anderson's morning newspaper is the ancestor of this page. The world map of publishers is a map of imagined communities.

books.title: Seeing Like a State
books.author: James C. Scott
books.question: What does the view from above fail to see about the lives it is counting?
books.why: A standing objection to any oracle, including this one. Legibility flattens.

books.title: The Great Transformation
books.author: Karl Polanyi
books.question: When markets are pulled loose from society, what moves to pull them back?
books.why: The double movement explains why a currency drop and a street protest can be the same story told twice.

books.title: The Future of Nostalgia
books.author: Svetlana Boym
books.question: Is this longing for a home that was, or for a home that never existed?
books.why: Boym separates restorative nostalgia, which rebuilds the lost home, from reflective nostalgia, which lingers on the ruins. Headlines do both.

books.title: Retromania
books.author: Simon Reynolds
books.question: When does a culture's return to its own past stop being a revival and become a holding pattern?
books.why: Reunion tours, revived slogans, retried verdicts. Reynolds asks what the present is avoiding.

books.title: Slow Violence and the Environmentalism of the Poor
books.author: Rob Nixon
books.question: Which harms are too slow to make a headline, and who pays for the delay?
books.why: A reservoir with forty days left is slow violence arriving on schedule.

books.title: A Theory of the Drone
books.author: Grégoire Chamayou
books.question: What happens to war, law and the idea of courage when one side can no longer be hit back?
books.why: The drone is the object this collection cannot stop mentioning. Chamayou is the clearest account of why it changes everything it touches.

books.title: Crowds and Power
books.author: Elias Canetti
books.question: What does a crowd want, and what does it become when it gets it?
books.why: A stadium, a square, an awards ceremony and a storming of parliament are all crowds. Canetti refuses to pretend they are unrelated.

books.title: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty
books.author: Albert O. Hirschman
books.question: When something is failing, do people leave it, shout at it, or stay and hope?
books.why: Sixty thousand voluntary departures and a student movement are the same choice, made in opposite directions.

books.title: How Democracies Die
books.author: Steven Levitsky and Daniel Ziblatt
books.question: Which unwritten rules keep an election from becoming a war, and what happens when they are tested abroad?
books.why: Election denial is now a script with a passport. This is the book on the guardrails it crosses.

books.title: The Light That Failed
books.author: Ivan Krastev and Stephen Holmes
books.question: What does it do to a country to spend thirty years imitating another?
books.why: The best account of why a student movement in Belgrade is read in Nairobi as a model, and why models resent being models.

books.title: Understanding Media
books.author: Marshall McLuhan
books.question: If the whole world watches the same thing at the same moment, what kind of village is that?
books.why: The night the Ballon d'Or appeared in ten countries' headlines was a McLuhan night.

books.title: The Society of the Spectacle
books.author: Guy Debord
books.question: When a ceremony is what we share instead of a fate, what has been traded for what?
books.why: Debord's spectacle is not entertainment. It is a social relation mediated by images. A world that agrees about a football is his world.

books.title: The Age of Surveillance Capitalism
books.author: Shoshana Zuboff
books.question: What is being sold when a company that watches goes public?
books.why: A prospectus is a company describing itself to money. Zuboff is the dictionary for reading it.

books.title: Social Acceleration
books.author: Hartmut Rosa
books.question: Why does a society that gets faster feel that it has less time?
books.why: Six in ten Dutch people said it was happening too quickly. Rosa says that sentence is the modern condition, not a complaint about one technology.

books.title: The Sense of an Ending
books.author: Frank Kermode
books.question: Why do we need the present to be the middle of a story, and what do we invent to make it one?
books.why: Kermode's tick-tock is this site's engine. Every reading here turns a tick into a tock. He explains why that is irresistible and why it is fiction.

books.title: Memory, History, Forgetting
books.author: Paul Ricoeur
books.question: What does a society owe to the past it chooses to reopen, and to the past it chooses to close?
books.why: A retrial after 47 years is a nation deciding what it is allowed to forget.

books.title: The Need for Roots
books.author: Simone Weil
books.question: What does a person need from a place in order to stay human in it?
books.why: Weil's list of the needs of the soul is the best reply to any reading that only counts crises. A choir is on her list.

books.title: New and Old Wars
books.author: Mary Kaldor
books.question: When a war has no front, no declaration and no end, what is it a war for?
books.why: Power stations, airports and churches are the battlefield now. Kaldor saw it coming.

books.title: The Invention of Tradition
books.author: Eric Hobsbawm and Terence Ranger
books.question: How old is this ritual really, and who benefits from its seeming older?
books.why: Halloween in Taipei, Auckland and Houston on the same weekend is an invented tradition going global in real time.

books.title: The Third Wave: Democratization in the Late Twentieth Century
books.author: Samuel P. Huntington
books.question: Why did so many countries learn to vote in the same thirty years, and what happens when a wave recedes?
books.why: Most of the countries reading each other’s results in 2026 democratised between 1974 and 1991. The book names the wave and warns about the undertow.

books.title: Risk Society: Towards a New Modernity
books.author: Ulrich Beck
books.question: What happens to a society that produces risks it cannot insure and then argues about who should bear them?
books.why: Written in the year of Chernobyl. A prospectus that lists extinction and asks for money is Beck’s argument in its purest form.

books.title: The Prize: The Epic Quest for Oil, Money, and Power
books.author: Daniel Yergin
books.question: How did a fuel become the organising fact of the twentieth century’s wars and alliances?
books.why: The Gulf’s two clocks run on the thing this book is about. Fifty years after 1973 the prize is still in the room.

books.title: The Shock of the Old: Technology and Global History since 1900
books.author: David Edgerton
books.question: Why do we tell the history of technology as a history of invention when most of what matters is use, maintenance and the old machines still running?
books.why: The frigate, the submarine and the rifle in the same collection as the drone. Edgerton explains why the two arms races coexist.

books.title: Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil
books.author: Hannah Arendt
books.question: What does evil look like when it is done at a desk, by a functionary, at a distance from its effects?
books.why: The question travels from a Jerusalem courtroom to a drone operator’s container and a militiaman’s tablet.

books.title: Media Events: The Live Broadcasting of History
books.author: Daniel Dayan and Elihu Katz
books.question: What happens when a society stops to watch itself watching: a coronation, a moon landing, a final?
books.why: The authors named the genre the Ballon d’Or belongs to. The link goes to the co-author’s page, which describes the book.

books.title: Postwar: A History of Europe Since 1945
books.author: Tony Judt
books.question: How was a continent rebuilt on an agreed forgetting, and what happened when the forgetting ended?
books.why: Judt’s argument that postwar Europe was founded on amnesia is the background to every retrial, exhumation and removed statue since.

books.title: The Age of Extremes: The Short Twentieth Century, 1914 to 1991
books.author: Eric Hobsbawm
books.question: What did the century between Sarajevo and the Soviet collapse actually change, and what merely happened?
books.why: Hobsbawm thought the cultural revolution of the 1960s outlasted every regime. The square, the camp and the dance in one week are its legacies.

books.title: Crashed: How a Decade of Financial Crises Changed the World
books.author: Adam Tooze
books.question: How did a crisis in American mortgages become a decade of politics everywhere?
books.why: The years after 2008 broke the housing compact between generations and moved manufacturing to the cheapest fab. Both facts are in this collection.

trajectories.title: Belgrade: students and a bulldozer bring down Milošević
trajectories.note: The Otpor student movement became the template that was exported, studied and resented across two decades. Serbia's students in 2026 are reading their own country's past.

trajectories.title: Brasília: Bolsonaro supporters storm the three powers
trajectories.note: Two years and two days after Washington, the same script ran in Brazil. By 2026 police in Jerusalem are preparing for it as a genre.

trajectories.title: Washington: the Capitol is stormed after a denied election
trajectories.note: The moment 'the election was rigged' stopped being a claim and became a plan. It has travelled since.

trajectories.title: Seoul: the head of the KCIA shoots President Park Chung-hee
trajectories.note: Forty-seven years to the day before this collection was gathered. A posthumous retrial asks whether the killer was a murderer or a democrat.

trajectories.title: Paris: France Football awards the first Ballon d'Or
trajectories.note: A magazine's end-of-year poll that became one of the few events the entire world reports on the same night.

trajectories.title: Palo Alto: the Theranos story begins to come apart
trajectories.note: A company valued on a future it had not built. The 2026 argument about one word in Elizabeth Holmes's defence is the long tail of that valuation.

trajectories.title: New York: Netscape goes public and prices the internet
trajectories.note: The first time the market was asked to put a number on a technology that would change everything and had not yet earned anything.

trajectories.title: Afghanistan: the first armed Predator strike
trajectories.note: The month the drone stopped being a camera and became a weapon. Everything it is now doing in Sudan, Saudi Arabia and Ukraine descends from this.

trajectories.title: The Gulf closes the tap: the Arab oil embargo
trajectories.note: The first lesson in how a regional conflict becomes a global price. Hormuz in 2026 is the same lesson with drones.

trajectories.title: Europe: the Springtime of Peoples
trajectories.note: Students and the young in forty cities, inspired by one another's newspapers, mostly defeated within a year. The precedent for every wave, and for every wave's ebb.

trajectories.title: North America: Halloween becomes a suburban children's festival
trajectories.note: A harvest festival rebuilt as a consumer ritual, then exported by film and retail until a Taipei fortune teller and a Wellington parent argue about it on the same weekend.

trajectories.title: Britain votes to leave the European Union
trajectories.note: A decade on, a British politician saying he wants to rejoin is a headline in Qatar. Decisions have afterlives.

trajectories.title: Nuremberg: a court tries a state for its war
trajectories.note: The origin of the idea that attacking civilians' infrastructure can be a crime rather than a tactic. A UN finding about Ukraine's power grid stands on it.

trajectories.title: London: the V-1, a bomb that flies itself
trajectories.note: The first pilotless weapon aimed at a city, launched by a state that could no longer spare pilots. The drone begins as a way of not being there.

trajectories.title: The Great Bitter Lake: Roosevelt meets Ibn Saud
trajectories.note: On the way home from Yalta the president and the king trade protection for oil on a cruiser. The bargain was never written down and has outlasted every treaty signed since.

trajectories.title: New Mexico: the first technology tested with an estimate that it might end the world
trajectories.note: Before the test a physicist checked whether the bomb could ignite the atmosphere. It was a state project, secret and tax-funded. The risk assessment preceded the prospectus by eighty years.

trajectories.title: Geneva: four conventions written in the shadow of the bombed city
trajectories.note: The postwar laws of war were drafted by people who had watched what aircraft did to Dresden, Tokyo and Hiroshima. Every argument about a power station struck from the air starts here.

trajectories.title: Baghdad: Iraq, Turkey, Iran, Pakistan and Britain sign a pact
trajectories.note: An anti-Soviet alliance of almost exactly the capitals reported meeting about regional security in 2026. It was written for Washington and died with the Iraqi monarchy in 1958.

trajectories.title: Paris: the first European Cup, a year before the Ballon d’Or and two before the Treaty of Rome
trajectories.note: Football’s Europe preceded the political one and was built for the same reason: to give people who had just fought each other something to meet about on a Wednesday night.

trajectories.title: Dartmouth: a workshop names artificial intelligence
trajectories.note: The field was named at a summer meeting funded by a foundation, in the decade when the state paid for everything that could change the world. Seventy years later the builder is a company.

trajectories.title: Suez: Britain’s role in the Middle East ends and America’s begins
trajectories.note: The moment the region learned that every settlement is underwritten by an outside power, and that the power can change.

trajectories.title: Sputnik: a satellite, a panic, and the founding of ARPA
trajectories.note: The American answer to a Soviet satellite was a research agency that later built the internet. For forty years the technologies that could change everything were commissioned by governments.

trajectories.title: Frankfurt: West Germany tries its own citizens for Auschwitz
trajectories.note: Eighteen years after the war, a state put its own people in the dock for what its courts had agreed to forget. The retrial as a national habit begins here.

trajectories.title: Brazil: the generals take power with Washington’s blessing
trajectories.note: An election abroad was somebody else’s business long before Nairobi and Athens read Lula’s result. For twenty-one years it was Washington’s.

trajectories.title: Paris: students, then ten million strikers
trajectories.note: The month that fixed the postwar script for the young in the square, and the state’s three replies: reform the university, clear the street, borrow the costume.

trajectories.title: Mexico City: the army fires on students ten days before the Olympics
trajectories.note: The other 1968. Where Paris reformed, Mexico closed the square. Antioquia’s curfew on minors is the mild descendant of this choice.

trajectories.title: Santiago: Allende wins and Washington sets out to make the economy scream
trajectories.note: The clearest case of a foreign power treating another country’s election as its own emergency. The market’s second vote was organised from abroad.

trajectories.title: Lisbon: the Carnation Revolution opens the third wave
trajectories.note: Spain, Greece, Latin America and then Eastern Europe followed. Most of the countries now reading each other’s results learned to vote in the same thirty years.

trajectories.title: Soweto: schoolchildren march against Afrikaans and begin the end of apartheid
trajectories.note: Fifty years of students ending governments starts here, in a country where the median age was eighteen.

trajectories.title: Geneva: Protocol I forbids attacking what civilians need to survive
trajectories.note: Article 54 names the things that may not be targeted: food, water, the works that supply them. A 1977 rule being applied in 2026 to drones over power stations.

trajectories.title: Tehran: the Shah falls and the year that redrew the Gulf begins
trajectories.note: The alliances meeting in 2026 were drawn in 1979: a revolution in February, a seized mosque in November, a Soviet invasion in December, and an American doctrine in January.

trajectories.title: Mecca: armed millenarians seize the Grand Mosque
trajectories.note: The Saudi state answered with thirty years of religious strictness, and later with a reversal. Any pact signed in Mecca is signed over this ground.

trajectories.title: Gwangju: the army kills hundreds of students and citizens
trajectories.note: Seven months after a KCIA chief shot the president, a general’s coup was answered by a city. Korea has been retrying 1979 and 1980 ever since.

trajectories.title: The Bekaa Valley: drones find and blind Syria’s air defences in an afternoon
trajectories.note: The first battle the object won. Israel’s decoys and cameras located the missiles and the air force did the rest. The export industry of 2026 descends from this day.

trajectories.title: Buenos Aires: Argentina tries its own juntas
trajectories.note: The first time since Nuremberg a state tried its own former rulers in its own courts, two years after they left. The age of transitional justice begins here.

trajectories.title: London and Philadelphia: a concert built to be watched by a billion people at once
trajectories.note: The first event designed as a simultaneous global audience. A football ceremony in nine countries’ headlines is its grandchild.

trajectories.title: Seoul: students and office workers win direct presidential elections
trajectories.note: The square worked. The country it produced is now the oldest in the constellation, and its young are in the exam hall rather than the street.

trajectories.title: Beijing: students fill the square and lose
trajectories.note: The same spring that won in Prague lost in Beijing. The civil service queue of ninety-seven applicants a place is what followed.

trajectories.title: England: the Premier League sells football by the season
trajectories.note: Satellite television turned a national league into a global product. A Lagos list of snubbed players is local news because of this.

trajectories.title: Luxembourg: the Bosman ruling frees footballers to move
trajectories.note: A European court turned national leagues into a global labour market. The migration story inside the sport story.

trajectories.title: Cape Town: the Truth and Reconciliation Commission trades amnesty for testimony
trajectories.note: A third way between the trial and the pardon. Every country that reopens its past since has had to choose among the three.

trajectories.title: Seoul: two former presidents sentenced for the 1979 coup and Gwangju
trajectories.note: Korea’s first re-sentencing of its dictatorship. One death sentence, two pardons the next year, and unfinished business that reopens in 2026.

trajectories.title: Jakarta: students occupy parliament and Suharto resigns after thirty-one years
trajectories.note: A leaderless student movement ended one of the longest rules of the century. Serbia’s students have a precedent in Southeast Asia as well as in Belgrade.

trajectories.title: London: Pinochet is arrested on a Spanish warrant
trajectories.note: The moment the past became prosecutable anywhere. A Chilean court reopening a 1996 case works in a legal world this arrest made.

trajectories.title: New York: the dot-com bubble bursts
trajectories.note: Five years of listings in which disclosure was no obstacle to belief, then a crash that produced the rules requiring a hundred pages of risk factors.

trajectories.title: Washington switches off the deliberate error in GPS
trajectories.note: The sky opened to civilians. Within a decade a Shenzhen company had put a camera on a quadcopter anyone could buy, and the drone stopped being a state’s thing.

trajectories.title: Brazil: Lula wins at the fourth attempt after the market votes first
trajectories.note: The real lost a third of its value before a ballot was cast and the candidate published a letter promising to honour the debt. The currency has voted in every Brazilian election since.

trajectories.title: The Hague: the International Criminal Court opens
trajectories.note: The high point of the belief that reopening the past could be institutionalised worldwide. What followed was reopening by other means: the archive stopped closing.

trajectories.title: Baghdad: the invasion removes Iran’s main enemy
trajectories.note: The export of elections became a security policy and discredited itself. Tehran gained a corridor to the Mediterranean, and Jordan a fault line it still lives on.

trajectories.title: Tbilisi: the Rose Revolution borrows Belgrade’s manual
trajectories.note: The first of the colour revolutions to copy Otpor directly. Russia’s answer, a theory that every crowd is somebody’s project, followed within a decade.

trajectories.title: New York: Lehman Brothers fails
trajectories.note: The crisis that pushed manufacturing to the cheapest fab, broke the housing compact between generations, and made the cloud the safest place to put money.

trajectories.title: Cairo: eighteen days in Tahrir Square
trajectories.note: The square won and lost within two years. The lesson the young of 2026 drew is visible in Belgrade: no leader to arrest, no party to co-opt.

trajectories.title: Madrid: the indignados camp in Puerta del Sol
trajectories.note: The same square as the 2026 camp. Last time the movement became a party, the party entered government, and the rents went up.

trajectories.title: Vienna: the Iran nuclear agreement
trajectories.note: The pact clock. Its abandonment in 2018 restarted the other one, and the region has alternated between the two at increasing speed since.

trajectories.title: #MeToo reopens cases prosecutors had closed
trajectories.note: A decade in which old verdicts were reopened from below, by testimony rather than by courts, and courts then had to catch up.

trajectories.title: Abqaiq: drones and missiles halve Saudi oil output for days
trajectories.note: The moment the cheap machine reached the most expensive target on earth. The airport headlines of 2026 are the same lesson applied to passengers.

trajectories.title: Bristol: a slave trader’s statue goes into the harbour
trajectories.note: The decade’s memory wars in one act. Statues, films, retrials and library shelves were all ways of re-sentencing the past.

trajectories.title: Nagorno-Karabakh: Turkish and Israeli drones win a war in forty-four days
trajectories.note: Every defence ministry rewrote its shopping list. The trade-fair headlines of 2026 are those lists being filled.

trajectories.title: Algiers: a referendum lets the army deploy abroad for the first time since 1973
trajectories.note: The constitutional change behind the 2026 headline about troops to Niger. The quiet redrawings happen in the Sahara.

trajectories.title: Europe: twelve clubs announce a closed league and lose to their own supporters in forty-eight hours
trajectories.note: The one time in the decade a crowd beat capital at its own game. The ceremony belongs to the clubs; the game, briefly, did not.

trajectories.title: Doha: a World Cup built by migrant workers
trajectories.note: The shared ceremony and the labour that builds it, in one tournament. The migration story the sport story usually leaves out.

trajectories.title: San Francisco: ChatGPT reaches a hundred million users in two months
trajectories.note: The demonstration became a market. The prospectus of 2026 is the market asking to be priced.

trajectories.title: A one-sentence statement: extinction from AI should be a global priority
trajectories.note: Signed by the heads of the laboratories building the thing. The risk factor in a 2026 prospectus is this sentence moved from an open letter into a legal filing.

trajectories.title: Dhaka: students over job quotas, then a prime minister on a helicopter
trajectories.note: The decade’s clearest case of students toppling a government. Serbia’s students had a precedent two years old.

trajectories.title: Novi Sad: a station canopy collapses and kills sixteen
trajectories.note: The beginning of the Serbian student movement that, by the headlines of October 2026, ended fourteen years of Vučić. It started with concrete, not ideology.

trajectories.title: Kathmandu: Gen Z protests under a pirate flag force out a government
trajectories.note: The flag was from a Japanese comic. The shared toys and the shared squares of the decade turned out to be the same network.

trajectories.title: Fordow: American bombers end a twelve-day Israel-Iran war
trajectories.note: The strike clock struck. Sixteen months later the same capitals are reported preparing again while a pact is drafted in Mecca.

trajectories.title: Russia: Ukrainian drones launched from parked lorries hit bombers thousands of kilometres from the front
trajectories.note: The cheapest machine against the most expensive. The arithmetic that makes Hezbollah plan a factory and Elbit sign a deal.

trajectories.title: Münster and Osnabrück: the Peace of Westphalia
trajectories.note: Rulers agreed that each would decide the religion of their own territory and stay out of their neighbours'. The sovereign state, and the right to be left alone inside its borders, dates from here.

trajectories.title: London: a royal charter for the East India Company
trajectories.note: A trading company with its own army, courts and taxes, governing a subcontinent for a century before the state took over. The company as a form of rule, and the trade route as a reason for empire.

trajectories.title: Waitangi: a treaty in two languages
trajectories.note: The English text ceded sovereignty; the Māori text promised something closer to governance while chiefs kept authority. Land disputes in New Zealand still turn on which version holds.

trajectories.title: Japan: the Meiji Restoration
trajectories.note: A country that had shut itself for two centuries took on railways, conscription, a constitution and factories within a generation, to avoid being colonised. The template for every state that industrialised to stay independent.

trajectories.title: Egypt: the Suez Canal opens
trajectories.note: A hundred miles of water that cut the voyage from Europe to Asia by weeks, financed in Paris, bought into by London, nationalised by Cairo in 1956. Every argument since about who owns a chokepoint runs through it.

trajectories.title: Berlin: Europe divides Africa on paper
trajectories.note: Fourteen states drew borders across a continent none of their delegates had crossed. Most of Africa's present frontiers, and many of its wars, follow those lines.

trajectories.title: Masjed Soleyman: oil is struck in Persia
trajectories.note: The first commercial oil in the Middle East, found by a British concession that became BP. Britain's navy switched to oil within six years, and the region has been read as a fuel supply since.

trajectories.title: London and Paris: the Sykes-Picot line
trajectories.note: Two diplomats divided the Ottoman Arab lands into British and French zones before the war that would deliver them was won. The borders of Iraq, Syria, Lebanon and Jordan, and the grievance that they were drawn elsewhere.

trajectories.title: Petrograd: the Russian Revolution
trajectories.note: A state that abolished private property and ran the whole economy from the centre, and then held for seventy years. Every twentieth-century argument about markets and the state was conducted with it in the room.

trajectories.title: Versailles: the treaty and the League of Nations
trajectories.note: Reparations, new states carved from three empires, and the first attempt at an assembly of nations to prevent the next war. It failed within twenty years, and 1945 was designed by people who had watched it fail.

trajectories.title: New York: the crash and the Depression that followed
trajectories.note: A quarter of American workers without jobs, world trade cut by two thirds behind tariffs, democracies falling in Europe. The reason governments since have treated a slump as something they must act against.
